title: Ceviche
subtitle: Peruvian raw fish cured in lime juice with chilli and red onion
excerpt: Very fresh white fish cut into small pieces and dressed with lime juice, red onion, coriander, and ají amarillo chilli. The lime juice denatures the surface proteins of the fish within minutes. Eaten immediately, cold and vivid.

recipe.sourceNotes: Ceviche has been eaten along the Pacific coast of South America for thousands of years, with the earliest evidence of marinated fish preparations found in coastal Peru dating back over two millennia. The modern Peruvian version, with lime juice, ají amarillo chilli, coriander, and red onion, became the standard form from the 20th century. Peru declared ceviche a national cultural heritage dish in 2004. The lime juice does not 'cook' the fish in the same way heat does: it denatures the proteins on the surface of the fish, turning it opaque, but does not kill all pathogens. Use sushi-grade or very fresh fish and serve within minutes of preparing.

content.text: The fish must be extremely fresh: sushi-grade if possible. Buy it on the day you plan to serve the ceviche and keep it well refrigerated until you need it. Cut the fish into small, even pieces of about 1 cm so the lime juice can work on them evenly. Dress and serve within 15 minutes: the longer it sits the more the fish overcures, losing its texture. The leche de tigre (tiger's milk) is the juices left at the bottom of the bowl after the fish is removed: it is considered a delicacy and is drunk as a shot.

content.text: Soak the sliced red onion in cold water for 10 minutes to take the edge off the sharpness. Drain and pat dry.
Put the fish in a chilled bowl. Add the garlic, ginger, chilli, salt, and lime juice. Stir gently. Leave to marinate for 5 to 10 minutes, no longer.
Add the drained red onion and coriander. Toss gently and taste for salt and lime. Serve immediately in chilled bowls with boiled sweet potato slices on the side if using.
